new_statements.quote: How should long vowels be interpreted phonologically? This may be seen as vowel length as it is, or as the phonetic manifestation of the stress (or accent) system as in the case of other Philippine languages (see Zorc 1993). Nevertheless, the present study demonstrates that it is phonologically the length of a vowel, rather than the phonetic manifestation of the stress system in two respects. [...] Since none of these two facts favour the long-vowel-as-stress analysis, this contrast will be treated more appropriately as the phonological long-short distinction of vowels. [p. 86 fn. 1:] This does not work in Arta since the language has no stress system (See §2.1.3).
new_statements.citation: Kimoto, Yukinori. 2017. A Grammar of Arta: A Philippine Negrito Language. PhD dissertation, Kyoto University (hdl 2433/226793; doi 10.14989/doctor.k20639).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Arta has no word stress/accent system. What looks like the penultimate 'accent' of other Philippine languages is phonemic vowel length (bi:lèg 'bracelet' vs bilèg 'fastness'; ana: 'child' vs a:na: 'children'): length is fixed to the root and never shifts under affixation (pe:nas > pe:nas-an, not pena:s-an), and a word may carry several long vowels with no primary/secondary asymmetry (ta:ta:me:ta, pe:be:bu:d=u). The inherited Proto-Philippine accent contrast was lost; Arta's long vowels arose independently by compensatory lengthening and vowel fusion, and stress in loanwords is reinterpreted as length.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None: the source argues explicitly that words with more than one long vowel show no primary/secondary prominence asymmetry (p. 52), which is one of its two reasons for rejecting a stress analysis.
new_statements.exceptions: Only an intonational, phrase-level phenomenon: at a clause boundary or utterance end speakers 'may stress the vowel of the final syllable by gaining its loudness and/or making it longer' (p. 42, 'emphatic stress', e.g. [dɔn.na.ba.gát]); this is not lexical word stress. Loanwords from Ilokano, Yogad, Spanish and English have their source stress reinterpreted as a long vowel; /e/ and /o/ are always long (pp. 51, 60-61).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (roots and affixed words, with citation and text forms); the only prominence described at phrase level is the final-syllable emphatic intonation. Author's field site: Nagtipunan, Quirino Province; ~10 native speakers.
new_statements.identity_note: Arta (glottocode arta1239, ISO atz), also called Edilod by its speakers per Kimoto's later titles; Kimoto's description is of the Arta of Nagtipunan, Quirino Province (about 10 native speakers, living among Casiguran Agta communities). Reid 1989 is based on a short 1987 elicitation and describes the same language. No separate dialects are distinguished in any source seen.

sources.locator: Ch. 2 Phonology, §2.1.3 'Syllable, mora, and vowel length', subsection 'Phonological status of vowel length in Arta', pp. 51-52 (PDF pp. 68-69 of the saved file); and Ch. 3 footnote 1, p. 86 (PDF p. 103). Same wording in Kimoto 2017 JSEALS SP1 §3.1, pp. 4-5.
sources.note: Ch. 2 Phonology, §2.1.3 'Syllable, mora, and vowel length' (pp. 50-56): vowel length is phonemic and is NOT the manifestation of a stress/accent system (length never shifts under affixation; several long vowels per word with no primary/secondary asymmetry); ch. 3 fn. 1 (p. 86): 'the language has no stress system (See §2.1.3)'; p. 42: only a phrase/utterance-final emphatic 'stressed intonation' (loudness/lengthening on the last syllable of the phrase); ch. 2 conclusion p. 83: the old Philippine accentual system has been lost in Arta.

sources.citation: Kimoto, Yukinori. 2017. Mora, Vowel Length, and Diachrony: the Case of Arta, a Philippine Negrito Language. In Hsiu-chuan Liao (ed.), Issues in Austronesian Historical Linguistics (JSEALS Special Publication No. 1), 1-22. Honolulu: University of Hawai'i Press.
sources.note: §3.1 'Phonological status of vowel length in Arta' (pp. 4-5 of chapter; PDF pp. 13-14 of the volume file): same argument as the dissertation — long vowels are phonological vowel length, not the phonetic manifestation of a stress (accent) system; abstract p. 1: Arta long vowels 'should be separated from inherited accents'; p. 12: source-language stress in loanwords is reinterpreted as vowel length.
